Safety, alignment, and trustworthiness of agentic systems remain largely unsolved, with governance frameworks still nascent
Forgetful but Faithful: A Cognitive Memory Architecture and Benchmark for Privacy-Aware Generative Agents (Paper 29)

research_gaps.title: Lack of Integration Between Biological Memory Fidelity and Engineering Performance
research_gaps.description: There is an unresolved tension between cognitive neuroscience-inspired memory designs and purely engineering-driven approaches, with no empirical consensus on whether biological fidelity (e.g., episodic/semantic/procedural distinctions, hippocampal-inspired indexing) actually improves practical agent performance over simpler engineered alternatives. Interdisciplinary barriers limit effective translation, and comparative studies directly testing bio-inspired vs. engineering-first designs are absent.
evidence: There is tension between cognitive neuroscience-inspired memory designs (Papers 1, 2, 5) and purely engineering-driven architectural approaches (Papers 4, 6, 9), with no consensus on whether biological fidelity improves practical agent performance
Interdisciplinary barriers between cognitive neuroscience and AI research limit the effective translation of biological memory concepts into practical AI architectures

Papers 1, 4, and 6 rely heavily on LLMs as the backbone for memory and reasoning, while Paper 3 and Paper 5 advocate for more structured, symbolic memory representations, suggesting a tension between neural/generative and structured/symbolic approaches
Biological memory models provide strong design inspiration, yet episodic memory integration with parametric LLM knowledge remains an open problem with no consensus solution

research_gaps.title: Multimodal Memory Integration for Long-Horizon Agents
research_gaps.description: While multimodal agents are increasingly common, robust long-term memory architectures that integrate vision, audio, and language over extended time horizons remain underdeveloped. Existing multimodal memory systems face unsolved challenges in cross-modal indexing, retrieval, and consolidation, and evaluation benchmarks for multimodal long-term memory are sparse. This gap is especially critical for embodied and companion agents operating in real-world environments.
evidence: Multimodal memory integration is nascent and not yet robustly evaluated across diverse modalities
Multimodal memory systems face challenges in efficiently indexing, retrieving, and consolidating heterogeneous data modalities over long time horizons
Game environments, while rich, may not fully generalize to real-world embodied agent scenarios
TeleMem: Building Long-Term and Multimodal Memory for Agentic AI (Paper 18); MemVerse: Multimodal Memory for Lifelong Learning Agents (Paper 20)

research_gaps.title: Scalability and Real-World Deployment of Long-Term Memory Architectures
research_gaps.description: Most long-term memory systems for LLM agents are evaluated in controlled, small-scale, or synthetic settings. Computational overhead of graph-based, neuro-symbolic, and hierarchical architectures at production scale, retrieval latency with growing memory stores, and the transition from research prototypes to real-world deployment remain largely unaddressed. There is a critical gap between laboratory demonstrations and production-ready systems serving diverse, large-scale user populations.
evidence: Computational overhead of graph-based and neuro-symbolic architectures may be prohibitive at scale
Scalability of memory stores as interaction history grows to very large sizes remains a challenge, with potential retrieval latency and storage cost issues

research_gaps.title: Human Oversight vs. Autonomy in Memory-Augmented Agentic Systems
research_gaps.description: There is an unresolved contradiction in the literature regarding how much human oversight should govern memory formation, retrieval, and use in autonomous agents. Some frameworks minimize human intervention as a design goal, while trustworthiness-focused work argues for robust human-in-the-loop governance. This tension is especially acute for long-term memory systems that accumulate sensitive, consequential knowledge over time, yet no empirical framework exists to calibrate the appropriate level of human control.
evidence: Papers differ on the degree of human oversight required: some frameworks emphasize minimal human guidance as a design goal, while trustworthiness-focused papers argue for robust human-in-the-loop governance and intervention mechanisms

Some papers advocate for autonomous, agent-driven memory organization, while others emphasize explicit user-profile construction driven by structured rules, reflecting disagreement on whether memory structuring should be emergent or engineered
Safety, alignment, and trustworthiness of agentic systems remain largely unsolved, with governance frameworks still nascent
Paper 1 emphasizes emergent social behavior from individual agent interactions as a key strength, while Paper 3's structured educational simulation imposes more top-down control over agent dynamics

hypotheses.title: LongMemBench: A Standardized Multi-Session, Multi-Modal Benchmark for Agent Long-Term Memory
hypotheses.description: We hypothesize that a unified benchmark spanning hundreds of real-world interaction sessions, diverse modalities (text, vision, audio), and multiple agent settings (embodied, conversational, task-oriented) will reveal systematic performance gaps across existing memory architectures that are invisible in short-horizon evaluations. Specifically, we predict that systems optimized for ≤5-session windows will degrade non-linearly in retrieval accuracy and task success beyond 50 sessions, and that no single architecture will dominate across all modalities and settings.
hypotheses.related_gap_title: Absence of Standardized, Long-Horizon Benchmarks for Agent Memory
hypotheses.suggested_methodology: Curate a benchmark dataset from real-world deployments (e.g., anonymized customer service logs, long-running personal assistant interactions, embodied robot task logs) spanning 100–500 sessions per agent. Define standardized metrics for memory fidelity, retrieval precision/recall, and downstream task performance. Establish a shared ontology for 'long-term memory' across agent types. Evaluate 5–10 representative memory architectures (RAG-based, graph-based, neuro-symbolic) under identical conditions, and release the benchmark publicly with a leaderboard to enable cross-system comparison.

hypotheses.title: Temporal Decay Tagging as a Scalable Proxy for Long-Horizon Memory Evaluation
hypotheses.description: We hypothesize that annotating memory entries with temporal relevance decay labels (derived from user re-access patterns and task outcome signals) can serve as a scalable, semi-automated mechanism for constructing long-horizon evaluation datasets without requiring full real-world deployment. This approach would enable the creation of realistic, large-scale benchmarks from existing interaction logs while providing a principled definition of 'memory importance' across agent types.
hypotheses.related_gap_title: Absence of Standardized, Long-Horizon Benchmarks for Agent Memory
hypotheses.suggested_methodology: Mine existing multi-session interaction datasets (e.g., dialogue corpora, customer support archives) and apply temporal decay annotation using a combination of user re-query signals, task success labels, and recency weighting. Train a lightweight relevance-decay classifier and use it to auto-label memory entries. Validate the resulting benchmark by measuring inter-annotator agreement with human experts and by testing whether decay-annotated retrieval improves downstream task performance in held-out agent evaluations.

hypotheses.title: Adaptive Forgetting Curves Improve LLM Agent Scalability Without Sacrificing Task Performance
hypotheses.description: We hypothesize that implementing biologically-inspired, task-adaptive forgetting curves—where memory decay rates are modulated by retrieval frequency, recency, and task relevance signals—will reduce memory store size by at least 40% compared to full-retention baselines while maintaining or improving downstream task performance. This directly tests whether principled forgetting can resolve the scalability-completeness tension without resorting to heuristic pruning.
hypotheses.related_gap_title: Unresolved Memory Consolidation, Forgetting, and Decay Mechanisms
hypotheses.suggested_methodology: Implement a parameterized forgetting module inspired by the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve and ACT-R memory decay, integrated into a RAG-based LLM agent. Train decay rate parameters using reinforcement learning signals from task success and user feedback. Compare against full-retention, random pruning, and LRU-cache baselines across multi-session benchmarks. Measure memory store size, retrieval latency, task success rate, and privacy exposure (as a proxy for sensitive data retention) across 50–200 session horizons.

hypotheses.title: Privacy-Preserving Selective Consolidation via Differential Privacy and Importance Scoring
hypotheses.description: We hypothesize that combining differential privacy mechanisms with importance-scored memory consolidation (where only high-utility, low-sensitivity memories are retained in long-term stores) can simultaneously satisfy right-to-be-forgotten compliance and maintain task performance within 5% of full-retention systems. This tests whether the privacy-completeness tension is resolvable through principled consolidation rather than ad hoc deletion.
hypotheses.related_gap_title: Unresolved Memory Consolidation, Forgetting, and Decay Mechanisms
hypotheses.suggested_methodology: Design a two-stage memory pipeline: (1) an importance scorer that ranks memories by task utility and sensitivity using a fine-tuned classifier, and (2) a differential privacy layer that adds calibrated noise to sensitive memory embeddings before consolidation. Evaluate on multi-session conversational and task-oriented benchmarks, measuring task success, memory footprint, and compliance with GDPR right-to-erasure requests (simulated via targeted deletion audits). Compare against full-retention and heuristic-pruning baselines.

hypotheses.title: Adversarial Memory Poisoning Attacks Systematically Degrade RAG-Based Agent Reliability
hypotheses.description: We hypothesize that targeted adversarial poisoning of as few as 1–3% of memory store entries in RAG-based LLM agents is sufficient to cause measurable, consistent behavioral manipulation (e.g., biased recommendations, factual errors, policy violations), and that current retrieval mechanisms provide no meaningful defense. This establishes the severity of the attack surface and motivates the development of security-aware memory architectures.
hypotheses.related_gap_title: Security and Adversarial Robustness of Agent Memory Systems
hypotheses.suggested_methodology: Develop a threat model for memory poisoning attacks (injection of adversarially crafted documents into external memory stores). Implement white-box and black-box attack variants targeting retrieval relevance scores. Evaluate attack success rate, behavioral manipulation severity, and detectability across 3–5 RAG-based agent systems on standardized QA and task-completion benchmarks. Measure the minimum poisoning rate required for reliable manipulation, and test naive defenses (e.g., perplexity filtering, embedding anomaly detection) to establish a security baseline.

hypotheses.title: Cryptographic Memory Provenance Tracking Reduces Adversarial Poisoning Success in Agent Memory Stores
hypotheses.description: We hypothesize that augmenting RAG-based memory architectures with cryptographic provenance chains (tracking the origin, modification history, and trust score of each memory entry) will reduce adversarial poisoning success rates by over 60% compared to unprotected baselines, with acceptable retrieval latency overhead (<15%). This tests whether security-aware memory design can be practically integrated into existing architectures.
hypotheses.related_gap_title: Security and Adversarial Robustness of Agent Memory Systems
hypotheses.suggested_methodology: Implement a provenance-aware memory store where each entry is tagged with a cryptographic hash of its source, insertion timestamp, and a trust score derived from source verification. Integrate a retrieval filter that down-weights low-trust or tampered entries. Evaluate against the poisoning attack suite developed in the companion hypothesis, measuring attack success rate, retrieval latency, and task performance degradation. Conduct ablation studies on trust score thresholds and provenance chain depth.

hypotheses.title: A Consent-Centric Memory Governance Framework Enables Compliant Persistent Agent Memory Without Performance Loss
hypotheses.description: We hypothesize that a structured consent management layer—where users explicitly define memory retention scopes, expiry policies, and deletion triggers at onboarding and throughout interaction—can be integrated into persistent agent memory systems without degrading task performance by more than 10%, while achieving full compliance with GDPR and CCPA data minimization and right-to-erasure requirements.
hypotheses.related_gap_title: Privacy and Ethical Governance of Persistent Personal Memory
hypotheses.suggested_methodology: Design and implement a consent management API that intercepts memory write operations, enforces user-defined retention policies, and supports on-demand erasure with cryptographic deletion verification. Integrate with an existing LLM agent memory framework (e.g., MemGPT or LangChain memory modules). Evaluate compliance via simulated regulatory audits, user comprehension of consent interfaces via user studies (n≥100), and task performance on multi-session benchmarks before and after consent-constrained memory pruning.

hypotheses.title: Federated Learning Enables Privacy-Preserving Personalization in Persistent Agent Memory Systems
hypotheses.description: We hypothesize that federated learning approaches, where personal memory representations are trained locally and only aggregated model updates (not raw memories) are shared, can achieve personalization performance within 8% of centralized memory systems while providing strong privacy guarantees (ε-differential privacy). This tests whether federated architectures can resolve the tension between personalization utility and data governance in production deployments.
hypotheses.related_gap_title: Privacy and Ethical Governance of Persistent Personal Memory
hypotheses.suggested_methodology: Implement a federated memory personalization system where each user's agent maintains a local memory encoder fine-tuned on personal interaction history. Use federated averaging with differential privacy noise injection to aggregate updates across users. Evaluate personalization quality (task success, preference alignment) against centralized and non-personalized baselines on a multi-user, multi-session benchmark. Measure privacy leakage via membership inference attacks and communication overhead per federation round.

hypotheses.title: Biologically-Inspired Episodic/Semantic Memory Separation Does Not Outperform Flat Vector Stores on Standard Agent Tasks
hypotheses.description: We hypothesize that, contrary to theoretical expectations, LLM agents using biologically-inspired memory architectures (episodic/semantic/procedural separation with hippocampal-inspired indexing) will not significantly outperform flat vector store baselines on standard task-completion and question-answering benchmarks, but will show advantages specifically in tasks requiring temporal reasoning and context-dependent recall. This tests the boundary conditions of biological fidelity's practical value.
hypotheses.related_gap_title: Lack of Integration Between Biological Memory Fidelity and Engineering Performance
hypotheses.suggested_methodology: Implement three memory architectures: (1) a biologically-inspired system with distinct episodic, semantic, and procedural stores and hippocampal-inspired indexing (e.g., complementary learning systems model), (2) a flat dense vector store (FAISS-based RAG), and (3) a hybrid. Evaluate all three on a diverse benchmark suite covering factual QA, multi-step task completion, temporal reasoning, and context-dependent recall across 10–100 session horizons. Use statistical equivalence testing to identify tasks where biological fidelity provides significant gains vs. no advantage.

hypotheses.title: Targeted Cognitive Neuroscience Primitives Selectively Improve Agent Memory Performance in High-Interference Scenarios
hypotheses.description: We hypothesize that selectively incorporating specific neuroscience-validated mechanisms—particularly pattern separation (to reduce memory interference) and memory reconsolidation (to update outdated memories)—into otherwise engineering-first architectures will yield measurable performance improvements in high-interference, long-horizon tasks, without requiring full biological fidelity. This identifies which biological primitives are worth engineering investment.
hypotheses.related_gap_title: Lack of Integration Between Biological Memory Fidelity and Engineering Performance
hypotheses.suggested_methodology: Conduct a modular ablation study: start with a strong engineering-first baseline (hierarchical RAG) and incrementally add individual neuroscience-inspired components (pattern separation via orthogonalized embeddings, reconsolidation via triggered memory update on retrieval). Evaluate each configuration on tasks specifically designed to induce memory interference (overlapping contexts, contradictory updates) and on standard benchmarks. Measure retrieval accuracy, task success, and computational overhead per added component to identify the highest-ROI biological primitives.

hypotheses.title: Cross-Modal Memory Indexing via Shared Latent Representations Enables Robust Long-Horizon Multimodal Retrieval
hypotheses.description: We hypothesize that training a unified cross-modal memory encoder—mapping vision, audio, and language inputs into a shared latent space with modality-agnostic indexing—will outperform modality-siloed memory systems by at least 20% on cross-modal retrieval tasks in long-horizon (50+ session) embodied agent benchmarks, while reducing memory store redundancy by eliminating duplicate cross-modal representations.
hypotheses.related_gap_title: Multimodal Memory Integration for Long-Horizon Agents
hypotheses.suggested_methodology: Fine-tune a multimodal encoder (e.g., ImageBind or a CLIP-based model extended to audio) on a diverse set of embodied agent interaction data to produce modality-agnostic memory embeddings. Implement a unified vector store with cross-modal retrieval queries. Evaluate against modality-siloed baselines (separate vision, audio, and text memory stores with late fusion) on a constructed long-horizon multimodal benchmark (100+ sessions, real-world embodied tasks). Measure cross-modal retrieval precision/recall, downstream task success, and memory store size.

hypotheses.title: Hierarchical Multimodal Memory Consolidation Reduces Storage Overhead While Preserving Long-Horizon Task Performance
hypotheses.description: We hypothesize that a hierarchical consolidation strategy—where raw multimodal sensory memories are progressively abstracted into modality-fused semantic summaries at increasing time scales (session → day → week)—will reduce multimodal memory store size by over 50% compared to full-retention systems while maintaining task performance within 10% on long-horizon embodied agent benchmarks.
hypotheses.related_gap_title: Multimodal Memory Integration for Long-Horizon Agents
hypotheses.suggested_methodology: Design a three-tier multimodal memory hierarchy: (1) raw sensory buffer (short-term), (2) session-level fused summaries (medium-term), (3) semantic concept store (long-term). Implement automated consolidation triggers based on temporal boundaries and retrieval frequency. Evaluate on a long-horizon embodied agent benchmark (e.g., simulated household robot tasks over 100+ sessions) measuring storage footprint, retrieval latency, and task success rate. Compare against flat full-retention and random-pruning multimodal baselines.

hypotheses.title: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Indexing with Adaptive Tiered Storage Resolves Retrieval Latency Scaling in Production Memory Systems
hypotheses.description: We hypothesize that a tiered memory architecture—combining fast approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexing for recent/high-frequency memories with compressed archival storage for older/low-frequency memories—will maintain retrieval latency below 100ms at memory stores exceeding 10 million entries, while preserving task performance within 5% of exact retrieval baselines. This directly addresses the scalability gap between research prototypes and production deployments.
hypotheses.related_gap_title: Scalability and Real-World Deployment of Long-Term Memory Architectures
hypotheses.suggested_methodology: Implement a tiered memory system using HNSW-based ANN indexing for the active tier and product-quantization-compressed embeddings for the archival tier, with an adaptive promotion/demotion policy based on retrieval frequency. Benchmark retrieval latency, memory footprint, and task performance at memory store sizes of 10K, 100K, 1M, and 10M entries using synthetic and real-world interaction logs. Compare against flat FAISS, exact k-NN, and graph-based memory baselines. Conduct load testing simulating concurrent multi-user production traffic.

hypotheses.title: Incremental Memory Updating Protocols Enable Continuous Deployment of Long-Term Agent Memory Without Full Re-Indexing
hypotheses.description: We hypothesize that incremental, append-friendly memory update protocols—where new memories are integrated into existing index structures without full re-indexing—will reduce memory update latency by over 70% compared to batch re-indexing approaches, enabling real-time memory updates in production deployments serving thousands of concurrent users without degrading retrieval quality.
hypotheses.related_gap_title: Scalability and Real-World Deployment of Long-Term Memory Architectures
hypotheses.suggested_methodology: Design and implement an incremental memory update protocol using dynamic HNSW graph insertion and lazy consolidation of memory clusters. Evaluate update latency, retrieval quality (precision/recall), and system throughput under simulated production load (1K–10K concurrent users) across memory stores of varying sizes. Compare against batch re-indexing, periodic snapshot, and no-update baselines. Measure degradation in retrieval quality over time as incremental updates accumulate, and test periodic re-consolidation as a corrective mechanism.

hypotheses.title: Empirically Calibrated Human Oversight Thresholds Improve Trust and Task Performance in Memory-Augmented Agents
hypotheses.description: We hypothesize that human oversight requirements for memory operations (formation, retrieval, and use) can be empirically calibrated based on memory sensitivity, task stakes, and agent confidence scores, such that a tiered oversight model (full autonomy → notification → approval) outperforms both fully autonomous and fully human-supervised baselines on a combined metric of task efficiency and user trust. This tests whether the autonomy-oversight tension can be resolved through adaptive, context-sensitive governance.
hypotheses.related_gap_title: Human Oversight vs. Autonomy in Memory-Augmented Agentic Systems
hypotheses.suggested_methodology: Develop a memory sensitivity classifier that scores each memory operation on axes of data sensitivity, task stakes, and agent confidence. Map scores to oversight tiers (autonomous, notify, require approval). Deploy in a user study (n≥150) where participants interact with memory-augmented agents under three conditions: fully autonomous, fully supervised, and adaptive tiered oversight. Measure task completion time, error rate, user trust (validated scales), and willingness to delegate across conditions. Use mixed-effects modeling to identify sensitivity/stakes thresholds that optimally balance efficiency and trust.

hypotheses.title: Explainable Memory Audit Trails Increase User Trust Without Significantly Reducing Agent Autonomy
hypotheses.description: We hypothesize that providing users with transparent, human-readable audit trails of agent memory operations (what was stored, retrieved, and why) will significantly increase user trust and perceived control in memory-augmented agents without requiring active human intervention in most memory operations, thereby resolving the autonomy-oversight tension through transparency rather than restriction.
hypotheses.related_gap_title: Human Oversight vs. Autonomy in Memory-Augmented Agentic Systems
hypotheses.suggested_methodology: Implement a memory audit trail module that generates natural language explanations for each memory write, retrieval, and deletion event, surfaced to users via a dashboard and in-context notifications. Conduct a randomized controlled user study (n≥200) comparing agents with and without audit trail access across long-horizon task scenarios. Measure user trust, perceived control, intervention frequency, task performance, and user satisfaction. Analyze which categories of memory operations trigger the most user interventions to identify where autonomy boundaries should be set.

findings.text: Finite context windows are a fundamental bottleneck for LLM agents in long-horizon tasks, necessitating external or structured memory architectures.
Biological memory models (episodic, working, semantic, short-term/long-term) provide strong design inspiration for LLM agent memory systems.
Episodic memory specifically enables single-shot, instance-specific learning and is argued to be the critical missing component for truly long-term LLM agents.
Unified or jointly managed long-term and short-term memory outperforms treating them as separate, heuristic-driven components.
Flat RAG / vector-database-only approaches are insufficient: they treat memory as a stateless lookup table, lack temporal continuity, and degrade with scale and noise.
Hierarchical and/or neuro-symbolic memory architectures (combining structured symbolic representations with neural retrieval) improve long-horizon reasoning over flat embeddings.
Graph-based memory representations (knowledge graphs, narrative graphs) improve coherence and relational reasoning but can introduce complexity and entanglement.
Lightweight memory orchestration strategies can match or exceed complex multi-stage pipelines while reducing computational overhead.
Narrative-driven or story-coherent memory organization (rather than fragmented embeddings) improves long-term conversational consistency.
Continuum Memory Architectures (CMA) introduce temporal continuity, write/update operations, and decay mechanisms absent in standard RAG.
Renormalization-group-inspired multi-scale memory abstraction enables modeling of long-term cross-session user state beyond fact-level retrieval.
Distributed, self-evolving memory systems (e.g., SEDM) address scalability in multi-agent settings by controlling noise accumulation and memory expansion.
Memory inflation and contextual degradation are specific failure modes in long-running agents (e.g., low-code/no-code business process agents), requiring active memory management policies.
Working memory frameworks from cognitive psychology, when applied to LLMs, improve complex sequential reasoning and task performance.
Integrating a scratchpad (reasoning trace) with dual short-term/long-term memory components (as in RAISE) enhances conversational agent coherence and task accuracy.

limitations: Most systems are evaluated on narrow benchmarks (e.g., household tasks, single-domain conversations) limiting generalizability.
Computational overhead of graph-based and neuro-symbolic architectures may be prohibitive at scale.
Flat RAG baselines are often used as the comparison point, potentially underrepresenting more sophisticated existing baselines.
Episodic memory integration with parametric LLM knowledge remains an open problem with no consensus solution.
Memory consolidation and forgetting mechanisms are underexplored; most systems lack principled decay or prioritization.
Multi-agent memory sharing (SEDM) introduces synchronization and consistency challenges not fully resolved.
Lightweight approaches (ENGRAM, LiCoMemory) may sacrifice recall precision for efficiency.
Narrative-driven memory (Amory) may struggle with non-narrative or highly factual/technical domains.
Working memory frameworks (Paper 13) are primarily validated on synthetic or constrained tasks.
Privacy and security implications of persistent long-term memory storage are largely unaddressed.
Temporal modeling in CMA and RGMem requires careful hyperparameter tuning (decay rates, abstraction levels).
Low-code/no-code agent memory management (Paper 11) is domain-specific and may not transfer to general agents.
contradictions: Graph-based memory is advocated as superior for relational reasoning (Papers 5, 7, 8, 9), but Papers 5 and 6 argue that flat or entangled graph structures introduce unnecessary complexity and that lightweight alternatives are preferable.
Papers 2 and 3 argue for unified/joint LTM-STM management, while Papers 13 and 14 treat them as distinct cognitive modules with separate roles, implying separation is beneficial.

Paper 1 positions episodic memory as the 'missing piece,' implying current architectures are fundamentally incomplete, while Papers 2, 4, 8, and 9 present their own systems as largely solving long-term memory challenges.

Paper 6 (ENGRAM) argues against complex multi-stage retrieval pipelines in favor of simplicity, while Papers 8 (Aeon) and 5 (LiCoMemory) advocate for sophisticated hierarchical/neuro-symbolic pipelines as necessary for performance.
RAG is treated as the baseline to surpass (Papers 4, 5, 8, 12), yet Papers 9 and 11 still rely heavily on retrieval-augmented approaches as core components of their proposed solutions.

findings.text: LLM-based autonomous agents require four core architectural components: memory, planning, action, and tool use/perception, which together enable complex, goal-directed behavior beyond static inference.

Cognitive neuroscience and human memory systems (e.g., episodic, semantic, procedural, working memory) serve as foundational inspiration for designing AI long-term memory architectures in autonomous agents.
Long-term memory is increasingly recognized as a critical capability gap in current LLMs, and bridging this gap is essential for agents to perform well on extended, real-world tasks.

Agentic AI represents a paradigm shift from reactive, prompt-response LLMs to proactive, autonomous systems capable of multi-step reasoning, planning, and self-directed action with minimal human guidance.
Decision-making in agentic frameworks integrates multiple reasoning strategies (e.g., ReAct, chain-of-thought, reflection) with memory augmentation and situational awareness to improve task outcomes.
Multi-agent systems and cloud-scalable architectures are emerging as necessary infrastructure for deploying agentic AI at world scale, enabling parallelism, specialization, and resilience.
Trustworthiness, safety, and governance are identified as critical cross-cutting concerns for real-world agentic AI deployment, requiring threat modeling, explainability, and policy frameworks.

There is a recognized lack of comprehensive, unified surveys and systematic frameworks for organizing the rapidly growing landscape of LLM agent research, motivating these survey and framework papers.
Reinforcement learning and symbolic reasoning are identified as complementary paradigms that, when integrated with LLMs, enhance autonomous decision-making and long-term planning capabilities.

Tool use and external resource integration (APIs, databases, the Internet) are essential for grounding LLM agents in real-world environments and extending their capabilities beyond parametric knowledge.

limitations: Interdisciplinary barriers between cognitive neuroscience and AI research limit the effective translation of biological memory concepts into practical AI architectures (Paper 2)
Most surveys acknowledge rapid pace of change in the field, meaning coverage may quickly become outdated (Papers 1, 3)
Lack of standardized benchmarks for evaluating long-term memory and autonomous agent performance across tasks (Papers 1, 3, 8)
Current LLMs have fundamental context-window and computational constraints that limit true long-term memory without external augmentation (Papers 1, 6)
Safety, alignment, and trustworthiness of agentic systems remain largely unsolved, with governance frameworks still nascent (Papers 7, 10)
Real-world deployment of agentic AI at scale faces latency, cost, and reliability challenges not fully addressed in current frameworks (Papers 9, 10)
Most proposed frameworks are theoretical or evaluated on narrow benchmarks, limiting generalizability to open-ended real-world tasks (Papers 5, 6, 8)
Explainability and interpretability of autonomous agent decision-making remain difficult, hindering trust and accountability (Papers 7, 10)
contradictions: Papers differ on the degree of human oversight required: some frameworks emphasize minimal human guidance as a design goal (Papers 7, 9), while trustworthiness-focused papers argue for robust human-in-the-loop governance and intervention mechanisms (Paper 10).

There is tension between cognitive neuroscience-inspired memory designs (Papers 1, 2, 5) and purely engineering-driven architectural approaches (Papers 4, 6, 9), with no consensus on whether biological fidelity improves practical agent performance.

Some papers frame reinforcement learning as a core component of agentic decision-making (Paper 7), while others treat LLM-native reasoning strategies (chain-of-thought, ReAct) as sufficient substitutes, implying disagreement on the necessity of RL (Papers 5, 8).

The scope of 'agentic AI' is inconsistently defined: some papers treat any LLM with tool use as an agent (Papers 6, 8), while others reserve the term for systems with persistent memory, autonomous goal-setting, and multi-step planning (Papers 7, 10).

findings.text: Fixed context windows are a fundamental bottleneck for LLMs in long-term, multi-session dialogues, and dedicated memory architectures are necessary to overcome this limitation.
Dynamic extraction, consolidation, and updating of memories (rather than naive full-history storage) significantly improves agent consistency and personalization over time.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) alone is insufficient for long-term personalization; it lacks reliable memory update, conflict resolution, and user-profile integration mechanisms.
Hierarchical or multi-layer memory architectures (e.g., short-term + long-term, episodic + semantic) outperform flat single-store approaches for personalized agent interactions.
Preference-aware and user-profile-driven memory updates lead to more informed, contextually grounded agent decisions compared to preference-agnostic memory systems.
Multimodal memory (integrating text, images, and other modalities) is an emerging requirement for next-generation long-term agentic AI systems.
Biologically inspired memory models (e.g., hippocampus-inspired, cognitive architectures) provide effective structural blueprints for designing AI memory systems.
Identity drift, hallucination propagation, and persona incoherence are critical failure modes in long-horizon generative agents that dedicated memory mechanisms can mitigate.
Autonomous memory augmentation—where agents self-organize and semantically structure growing memory stores—improves scalability and retrieval precision.
Memory systems must support migration across platforms (virtual and robotic) and adapt to evolving environmental contexts for true long-term companionship.

limitations: Most systems are evaluated on synthetic or limited real-world datasets, raising questions about generalizability to diverse real-world long-term interactions.
Scalability of memory stores as interaction history grows to very large sizes remains a challenge, with potential retrieval latency and storage cost issues.
Conflict resolution between contradictory or outdated memories is not fully solved; most systems handle it heuristically.
Multimodal memory integration is nascent and not yet robustly evaluated across diverse modalities.
Privacy and ethical concerns around storing detailed personal user data over long periods are acknowledged but not deeply addressed.
Preference-aware updates may introduce bias if user preferences are inferred incorrectly or change over time.
Biologically inspired models (e.g., hippocampus-based) are approximations and may not fully capture the complexity of human memory.
Platform migration for companion agents (Paper 10) is an early-stage model with limited empirical validation.
Identity coherence mechanisms (ID-RAG) are primarily evaluated in controlled multi-agent settings and may not generalize.
Most frameworks focus on text-based interactions; robustness to noisy, real-world conversational input is underexplored.
contradictions: RAG is positioned as a baseline solution to long-term memory in some papers (Papers 5, 8) but is simultaneously critiqued as fundamentally insufficient for personalization without augmentation (Papers 7, 9), creating tension about whether RAG is a viable foundation or a flawed starting point.

Paper 10 (2009) proposes a relatively simple event-salience-based memory model for companions, while later papers (e.g., Papers 6, 7) argue that hierarchical, semantically rich multi-layer architectures are necessary—implying the earlier approach is inadequate, though it was never directly refuted in the cluster.

Some papers advocate for autonomous, agent-driven memory organization (Paper 4), while others emphasize explicit user-profile construction driven by structured rules (Paper 8), reflecting disagreement on whether memory structuring should be emergent or engineered.

Papers 5 and 6 treat multimodal memory as essential for future-ready agents, while the majority of the cluster (Papers 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9) focus exclusively on text-based memory, implying an unresolved scope disagreement about what 'long-term memory' must encompass.

findings.text: Existing benchmarks for long-term conversational memory are limited in scope, typically covering no more than five chat sessions, leaving very long-term dialogue evaluation largely unexplored.
Memory hallucinations — including fabrication, errors, conflicts, and omissions — are a frequent and underexplored failure mode in agent memory systems during storage and retrieval.
Privacy is a critical but underaddressed concern in agent memory management; unlimited memory stores create both computational intractability and privacy risks.

Different types of memory (e.g., episodic, semantic, procedural) vary in effectiveness for long-context conversational tasks, and systematic comparison is needed to identify the most effective approaches.
AI Clone memory systems require richer, more continuous personal data (experiences, emotions, opinions) beyond simple conversational histories, which current benchmarks fail to capture.

Intelligent agents operating in partially-observed 3D environments require long-term spatial memory (object positions, room layouts) to reason and navigate effectively, and dedicated benchmarks are needed to evaluate this.
RAG and long-context LLMs show promise for long-term dialogue but their efficacy in very extended conversational settings has not been rigorously evaluated.
Cognitive-inspired memory architectures that selectively forget information can improve both performance and privacy compliance in generative agents.

limitations: Most benchmarks rely on synthetic or curated data that may not reflect real-world conversational complexity or diversity (Papers 1, 2, 3).
Evaluation of very long-term memory (hundreds of sessions) is computationally expensive and difficult to scale (Papers 1, 5).
Hallucination evaluation frameworks may not generalize across all memory architectures or agent types (Paper 4).
Privacy-aware forgetting mechanisms may trade off memory fidelity for privacy, potentially degrading task performance (Paper 5).
Spatial memory benchmarks in 3D mazes may not transfer to real-world embodied agent scenarios (Paper 6).
AI Clone benchmarks depend on availability of rich, longitudinal personal data, raising ethical and data collection challenges (Paper 2).
Existing evaluations often focus on a single memory type or modality, limiting cross-type comparisons (Paper 3).
contradictions: Papers 1 and 3 both address long-term conversational memory evaluation but differ in emphasis: Paper 1 focuses on the lack of very long-term benchmarks (>5 sessions), while Paper 3 suggests the core gap is not benchmark length but rather the unclear relative effectiveness of different memory types — implying the problem is architectural, not just evaluative.

Paper 5 advocates for selective forgetting (privacy-aware memory pruning) as beneficial, while Papers 1 and 3 implicitly treat more complete memory retention as desirable for conversational continuity — creating a tension between memory completeness and privacy/efficiency.

Paper 6 evaluates memory in embodied/spatial settings (3D mazes), which operates under fundamentally different assumptions than the text-based conversational memory evaluated in Papers 1–5, suggesting the field lacks a unified definition of 'long-term memory' for agents.

findings.text: Structuring agent memory into distinct cognitive subsystems (short-term, episodic, semantic) inspired by human cognitive science significantly improves agent performance and believability.
Knowledge graphs are an effective representational substrate for modeling multiple memory types (short-term, episodic, semantic) in AI agents.
Generative agents equipped with memory streams, reflection, and retrieval mechanisms can simulate believable, coherent human-like behavior in interactive environments.
Multimodal memory architectures (combining vision and language) are necessary for lifelong learning agents to avoid catastrophic forgetting and support long-horizon reasoning.
Dual memory systems (combining short-term and long-term memory) enable LLM-based agents to simulate complex, high-fidelity human systems such as educational dynamics.

Memory-augmented frameworks leveraging both semantic and episodic memory allow agents to learn classification tasks from labeled examples without parameter updates, offering a cost-effective alternative to fine-tuning.

Episodic memory is identified as a critical component for continual learning agents that must accumulate experience over their operational lifetime and communicate learnings to other agents or humans.
Reflection and self-evolution mechanisms built on top of memory systems enhance agent adaptability and learning over time.

limitations: Generative agents are computationally expensive and may produce occasional incoherent or implausible behaviors due to LLM hallucination (Paper 1).
Knowledge graph-based memory systems may struggle to scale to complex, high-dimensional real-world environments (Paper 3).
Episodic memory proposals remain largely theoretical/conceptual without full empirical validation at scale (Paper 5).
Multimodal memory systems face challenges in efficiently indexing, retrieving, and consolidating heterogeneous data modalities over long time horizons (Paper 2).
LLM-based educational simulation agents may not fully capture the nuanced dynamics of real classroom interactions (Paper 4).
Memory-augmented classification frameworks without parameter updates may underperform fine-tuned models on complex or distribution-shifted tasks (Paper 6).
Most systems are evaluated in controlled or simulated environments, limiting generalizability to open-world deployment.
contradictions: Papers 1, 4, and 6 rely heavily on LLMs as the backbone for memory and reasoning, implicitly assuming LLM capabilities are sufficient; Paper 3 and Paper 5 advocate for more structured, symbolic memory representations (knowledge graphs, explicit episodic stores), suggesting a tension between neural/generative and structured/symbolic approaches.

Paper 6 argues that parameter-free, memory-augmented learning is a viable and preferable alternative to fine-tuning, while the broader literature (implicitly referenced in Papers 1 and 2) suggests that parameter updates remain important for deep adaptation — a potential conflict in how 'learning' is defined.

Paper 5 (2020) proposes episodic memory as a future research direction, while Papers 1 (2023), 2 (2025), and 6 (2025) have already operationalized episodic-like memory in working systems, reflecting a rapid shift from proposal to implementation that may make some of Paper 5's framing outdated.

findings.text: Experience-driven memory combined with look-ahead action simulation enables LLM agents to adapt to unseen web environments without fine-tuning, producing more efficient action sequences for long-horizon web navigation.
Memory sharing across LLM-based agents improves task performance by broadening the diversity and comprehensiveness of examples available at inference time, reducing divergence from expected outputs.
RAG-based memory mechanisms in LLM agents are vulnerable to adversarial poisoning attacks (AgentPoison), where malicious content injected into memory or knowledge bases can manipulate agent behavior.
Transitioning from static context windows to dynamic, retrieval-augmented memory architectures significantly improves long-term coherence and contextual relevance in conversational AI systems.
RAG mechanisms are a dominant paradigm for external memory in LLM agents, used across diverse applications including web navigation, multi-agent collaboration, and conversational AI.

LLM agents relying on memory modules or RAG are susceptible to security threats; adversarial triggers can reliably redirect agent actions toward attacker-specified targets across multiple agent frameworks.
Agriculture and domain-specific data sharing represents an emerging application area for RAG-driven conversational memory architectures.

limitations: WebATLAS may still struggle with highly dynamic or novel web environments not represented in prior experience memory (Paper 1)
Memory sharing approaches depend on the quality and relevance of shared memories; poor or mismatched memories from other agents could degrade performance (Paper 2)
AgentPoison's attack success may vary across agent architectures and retrieval strategies; defenses against such poisoning remain underexplored (Paper 3)

The literature review is limited by the recency and coverage of published work on RAG memory architectures, and agriculture-specific implementations remain largely theoretical or early-stage (Paper 4)

Most evaluations are conducted in controlled or benchmark environments, limiting generalizability to real-world deployments (Papers 1, 2, 3)
contradictions: Papers 1 and 2 implicitly assume that richer, shared, or experience-based memory improves agent reliability and safety, while Paper 3 directly challenges this assumption by demonstrating that memory modules are a critical attack surface — more capable memory does not inherently mean more secure agents.

Paper 4 advocates for broader adoption of RAG-driven memory architectures for coherence and scalability, while Paper 3 raises concerns that widespread RAG adoption without security safeguards introduces systemic vulnerabilities, creating a tension between capability and safety.

findings.text: LLM-based game agents serve as a valuable testbed for exploring capabilities relevant to Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), as game environments provide rich, controllable, and complex settings that mirror real-world challenges.

The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) provides new opportunities to endow game agents with generalizable reasoning, planning, and decision-making capabilities beyond traditional rule-based or narrow ML approaches.
Memory mechanisms are a critical component of LLM-based game agents, enabling them to retain and retrieve past experiences, context, and knowledge to inform future actions in dynamic environments.
Game agents built on LLMs demonstrate multimodal and embodied characteristics, integrating perception, action, and memory in interactive environments.

contradictions: With only one paper in the cluster, no direct contradictions between papers can be identified. However, within the broader field, there is ongoing debate about whether game-based benchmarks truly reflect AGI-level generalization or merely measure narrow task performance.

findings.text: Generative agents powered by LLMs can simulate believable human behavior, including daily routines and social interactions, enabling rich interactive simulations.

LLM-based agents demonstrate generalizable reasoning and planning capabilities that transfer across specialized domains including social simulation, web navigation, education, and gaming.

limitations: Generative agents are computationally expensive and may not scale to very large populations or real-time applications (Paper 1)
WebATLAS may still struggle with highly dynamic or adversarial web environments not covered by prior experience (Paper 2)
The AI-Agent School simulation may not fully capture the nuanced complexity of real-world educational interactions and teacher-student dynamics (Paper 3)

contradictions: Paper 2 suggests that fine-tuning on environment-specific data is unnecessary when experience-driven memory is used, while Paper 4 implies that domain-specific adaptation (including fine-tuning) remains important for robust game agent performance—suggesting tension about the sufficiency of in-context/memory-based approaches versus parameter-level adaptation.

Paper 1 emphasizes emergent social behavior from individual agent interactions as a key strength, while Paper 3's structured educational simulation imposes more top-down control over agent dynamics, reflecting differing philosophies on how much structure should govern agent behavior in simulations.
